html:
The most intense tropical cyclone on record in the North Indian Ocean, which hit the coast of Odisha (then Orissa) in eastern India on 29 October 1999. It killed about ten thousand people.

Winds of around 250 kilometres an hour and a storm surge several metres high swept over the low coast near Paradip. The storm then stalled over land for two days, pouring rain and flooding huge areas. Villages of mud and thatch were flattened, millions lost homes and crops, and many died because warnings did not reach them or there was nowhere safe to go.

The disaster changed how India deals with storms. Odisha set up the country's first state disaster management authority, built hundreds of concrete cyclone shelters along the coast, and trained local people to run evacuations. When Cyclone Phailin, of similar strength, struck in 2013, close to a million people were moved in time and few died. The approach drew praise worldwide, in the same way that Bangladesh learned from the Bhola cyclone of 1970. Burma, without such preparation, lost over 130,000 people to Cyclone Nargis in 2008.
sum: The most intense tropical cyclone on record in the North Indian Ocean, which hit the coast of Odisha (then Orissa) in eastern India on 29 October 1999. It killed about ten thousand people.
